planting.note: Plant bare-root or containerized trees in early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Eta is grown chiefly as a pollenizer and should be interplanted at roughly one tree per eight to ten producing trees to overlap bloom with the main harvest cultivar.

directions: Eta is a pollenizer selection from the Oregon State University hazelnut breeding program, released to supply reliable, compatible pollen for eastern filbert blight-resistant orchards planted to cultivars such as Jefferson and Yamhill. It carries strong resistance to eastern filbert blight and sheds pollen over an extended window, improving nut set in commercial and home plantings alike. Because it is grown for catkins rather than a marketable nut crop, prune lightly to maintain an open habit with abundant flowering wood and site it upwind of the cultivars it is meant to pollinate.
sources: Oregon State University Department of Horticulture hazelnut breeding program

planting.note: Plant bare-root or containerized trees in early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Gamma is grown as a pollenizer and should be distributed through the orchard so its bloom overlaps that of the harvested cultivar.

directions: Gamma is another eastern filbert blight-resistant pollenizer from the Oregon State University hazelnut breeding program, developed to keep pollen supply reliable as growers replaced blight-susceptible pollenizers like Daviana in modern EFB-resistant orchards. Its bloom period is timed to overlap with widely planted cultivars, and its resistance means it will not become a disease reservoir the way older susceptible pollenizers could. Like other pollenizer selections, its own nuts are secondary; focus management on maintaining vigorous flowering wood rather than nut size or cluster count.
sources: Oregon State University Department of Horticulture hazelnut breeding program

planting.note: Plant grafted trees while dormant in deep, well-drained soil well away from garden beds, since black walnut roots exude growth-inhibiting juglone.

directions: Football is a long-cultivated named black walnut selection valued for its distinctly elongated, football-shaped nuts, which are noticeably larger than typical wild seedling nuts and crack out in good-sized kernel pieces. It has circulated through nut grower collections and variety trials for decades as a reliable producer once established on grafted rootstock. Give it wide open spacing in full sun and deep soil, and keep it away from vegetable gardens, fruit trees, and other juglone-sensitive plantings.
sources: University of Missouri Center for Agroforestry

planting.note: Plant grafted or bare-root trees in early spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Imshu benefits from a second heartnut nearby to improve pollination and fill.

directions: Imshu is a long-established named heartnut selection prized among nut growers for heavy, consistent production and nuts that split cleanly along the suture to release a whole heart-shaped kernel with relatively little effort. It bears in long clusters typical of heartnut and tends to come into production somewhat earlier than seedling trees. As with all heartnuts, it is far less allelopathic than black walnut, so it can be sited closer to garden plantings, though it still benefits from deep, fertile, well-drained soil and full sun.
sources: University of Missouri Center for Agroforestry

planting.note: Plant grafted or bare-root trees in early spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun; pair with another heartnut cultivar to ensure good pollination and consistent kernel fill.

directions: Wright is a named heartnut cultivar recognized in nut grower circles for ripening earlier in the season than many other heartnut selections, along with good cracking quality and a clean kernel release. Early ripening makes it a useful choice in shorter-season northern locations where later heartnut selections may not fully mature before fall frosts. Provide the same deep, well-drained soil and full sun that other heartnuts and walnuts require, and expect grafted trees to begin bearing within four to seven years.

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in fall or early spring into deep, moist, well-drained bottomland-type soil in full sun; shellbark hickory develops a long taproot and transplants best while young with minimal root disturbance.

directions: Keystone is a named shellbark hickory selection valued by nut tree enthusiasts for producing the largest nuts of any North American hickory in a shell that, while still thick, cracks out with better kernel recovery than typical wild seedling shellbarks. Like all shellbark hickories it prefers deep, moist, fertile bottomland-type soils and tolerates wetter sites than shagbark hickory. Grafted trees are slow to reach bearing age, often a decade or more, but produce sweet, richly flavored kernels once established, making this a long-term planting for patient collectors.
sources: University of Missouri Center for Agroforestry
